title: Trichomes, Floral Maturity and Representative Harvest Assessment

content.overview: Glandular trichomes and floral structures change during maturation, but development can vary among cultivars and across locations on the same plant. Harvest assessment should therefore use repeated, representative observations rather than a single top flower or fixed amber percentage.

vocabulary.definition: A resin-producing epidermal structure found prominently on cannabis floral tissues.
An observation or sample selected to reflect the broader crop rather than an extreme location.
Uneven maturation among tissues, flowers, canopy positions, or plants.

sections.title: Trichomes change with age
sections.body: Trichome morphology and appearance evolve through development, providing useful maturity information when observations are made consistently.

sections.title: Color is not a universal clock
sections.body: Clear, cloudy, and amber appearance can vary with genotype, tissue type, plant age, and observation method. No single percentage should be treated as a universal harvest threshold.

sections.title: Sampling position matters
sections.body: Upper flowers can mature differently from shaded lower positions. Use comparable tissues at multiple representative canopy locations and repeat observations over time.

sections.title: Combine multiple indicators
sections.body: Floral structure, trichome observations, plant condition, developmental trend, and quality objective should be considered together. Multiple lines of evidence reduce overconfidence in one indicator.

workedExamples: If top flowers show more amber trichomes than the middle canopy, record both rather than harvesting from the top observation alone.
If the advertised flowering week has arrived but representative floral observations are still changing rapidly, continue evaluating the plant rather than using the calendar as the only rule.
commonMistakes: Sampling only sugar leaves instead of comparable floral tissues.
Using one magnified image to represent the entire plant.
Applying a universal amber percentage across cultivars.
content.practicalApplication: Define representative sampling locations and tissue type, use the same magnification method, record trichome and floral-development observations on several dates, and make the harvest decision from the trend and crop objective.
content.summary: Maturity assessment is a sampling problem as much as an observation problem. Repeated representative floral and trichome data are stronger than fixed week counts or one color threshold.
